The cheapest line on your AWS bill is the one you're arguing about

One production support app running on Claude Sonnet costs about $29,800 a month in tokens. The ten terabytes of data feeding a system like that costs about $230 a month in S3 Standard — roughly $23 per terabyte. Two lines on the same invoice, and the inference runs on the order of 130x the storage, every month, forever.

That ratio is the whole point, so it's worth drawing it to scale before we argue about anything.

The storage bill, to scale

S3 Standard is $0.023 per GB-month for the first 50 TB. A terabyte is about twenty-three dollars. Ten terabytes is $230 a month, $2,760 a year. The vector layer that sits on top — the part that makes retrieval work — is where it gets almost comic: 10 million vectors in a managed vector database (Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant) runs $850 to $5,000+ a month. The same 10 million vectors stored as raw S3 vectors: $1.38 a month. Not a typo. A dollar thirty-eight.

Now put the token bill next to it. One app on Sonnet: ~$29,800/month. Real enterprise API bills land between $50,000 and over $1,000,000 a month. And RAG makes it worse — a retrieval-augmented query burns three to five times the tokens of a plain one, because you're stuffing retrieved context into every prompt.

So the honest, like-for-like comparison — infrastructure against infrastructure, no salaries smuggled in on either side — is $29,800 of tokens against $230 of storage. The storage is a rounding error. It was always a rounding error.

The egress fear — and why it mostly doesn't apply here

The complaint was never really about storage. It's about egress — the fee to move data out to the public internet. Storing a gigabyte costs $0.023 a month; sending that same gigabyte out to the internet runs $0.09 past the first 100 GB each month. That charge tracks how much data leaves for the internet, not how much you keep, which is why it's the line teams forecast worst and the number-one reason a bill lands at two to three times the pricing page.

But look at where the data actually goes in a GenAI stack. If your S3 bucket and the services reading it — Amazon Bedrock, SageMaker, whatever's running inference — sit in the same region, that transfer is free. Same-region S3-to-service data transfer carries no charge at all. Put a VPC gateway endpoint in front of S3 and the traffic never leaves AWS's private network: no internet gateway, no NAT (which would otherwise run $0.045/GB), no data-transfer charge. The gateway endpoint itself costs nothing to run.

So for exactly the architecture this piece is about — data in S3, read in-region by Bedrock or SageMaker inside a VPC — the egress bill that gives S3 its scary reputation is zero. The fear is real for public-internet and cross-region traffic, and worth designing around if you have it. It simply isn't in the picture for a well-built in-region pipeline. Which leaves the token bill as the whole story, again.

What the zero-egress pipeline actually looks like

Walk the green arrows. S3 holds the data. A VPC gateway endpoint is the private door from your subnets to S3 — traffic rides AWS's own network, never the public internet. The agent runtime orchestrates from inside the VPC: it chunks and embeds through Lambda and Bedrock, retrieves the top-k matches from the vector store (OpenSearch Serverless, or S3 Vectors at about $1.38 a month for 10 million vectors), builds the prompt, and calls the model. Every green arrow stays in-region and on the private network, so the data-transfer line is zero.

Two things decide whether you actually get that zero, and both are easy to miss. First, same region: gateway endpoints are same-region only — by design they're route-table based and can't point outside the region — so a bucket in one region and a Bedrock VPC in another means the endpoint can't help you, traffic falls back to NAT, and you pay. Keep the bucket and the compute in the same region. Second, the route-table association: creating the gateway endpoint is not the step people think it is. If a subnet's route table is missing the endpoint's prefix-list route, that subnet's S3 traffic quietly goes out through the NAT gateway instead — $0.045 per GB, no error thrown, forever. The tell that someone has actually shipped this is that they open each subnet's route table and confirm the S3 prefix-list entry is there. "I created the endpoint" is not "the traffic is using it."

Where the money actually goes when it goes

MIT's State of AI in Business 2025 found that 95% of GenAI pilots delivered no measurable P&L impact, against an estimated $30–40 billion poured in. Gartner expects more than 30% of GenAI projects to be abandoned after the proof-of-concept stage. A completed-but-failed enterprise AI project costs, on average, $6.8 million and returns $1.9 million — a negative 72% ROI — and implementations routinely run three to five times their initial estimate, precisely because "negligible per-token cost" during a pilot becomes a real number when it's multiplied across thousands of users.

Set that against the storage line one more time: the $2,760 a year of S3 you were auditing is four one-hundredths of one percent of a single $6.8M failed project. You could keep that ten terabytes for over two thousand years for the cost of one dead POC.

The expensive side is the side worth engineering

If the storage line is a rounding error and the token line is the real number, then the work worth doing is on the token side — and that's the side we spend our days on. The failure mode in the MIT data isn't "the model was too dumb"; it's that teams could build an agent in a notebook and then couldn't ship it, govern it, or control what it cost once real traffic hit. That gap — prototype to governed production — is the whole product.

What that looks like with a number attached: Dairyland Power, an energy cooperative, had foremen spending one to two hours per work order pulling safety clauses by hand, across 100+ work orders a day. The agent brought that to about five minutes — 70,000+ hours a year, which the case study puts at roughly $1.5 million in annual savings. It runs in the customer's own cloud (their data never leaves it), under SOC2, GDPR, and ISO 27001, with a reflection step to hold down hallucination on safety-critical output. A separate deployment at a global IT firm cut high-priority incidents by 80%.

The reason to name those specifics isn't the logo. It's that they're the answer to the cost problem this whole piece is about: the expensive part of the stack is inference and the operational scaffolding around it, so that's where cost control, auto-scaling, and governance have to live — not in a spreadsheet arguing about gigabytes. Register the agents, put policy and observability and cost controls around them, and the token bill becomes something you manage instead of something that surprises you in month three.

And the model call itself is a cost lever, not a fixed price. The platform can call a foundation model directly or route the same agent through Amazon Bedrock — you choose the path per workload on outcome and cost, rather than hard-wiring one endpoint and living with its bill. That's the real value of running the platform on AWS: the freedom to focus on the outcome and still pick the cost winner for each job, on the substrate that already gives you the zero-egress data path above.

So — do the basics still matter?

Yes. That's not a caveat, it's the conclusion. The reason the S3 bill is a rounding error is that storage, done properly, is cheap and boring and reliable — and the reason so many GenAI projects burn millions is that the boring parts underneath them weren't done properly. Well-organized data is what makes retrieval work; retrieval quality is your data quality wearing a new coat. The fundamentals didn't stop mattering when the models got expensive. They started mattering more, because now a sloppy foundation doesn't just cost you a slow query — it costs you a seven-figure pilot that never ships.

Keep the data in-region so egress never enters the picture, watch the token bill, and stop auditing the cheapest, most reliable line on the invoice.
